If push protection blocks a recording, screenshot, transcript, or fixture:

Stop the push and read the reported file and commit locations. Do not paste the secret into an issue,
pull request, or bypass explanation.

If the value is a real credential, revoke or rotate it with its provider immediately. Remove it from the
recording and every local commit being pushed; deleting it only in a later commit leaves it in history.

Replace the recording with a redacted version or record it again with dummy values. Keep credentials in
environment variables outside the recording, and inspect the replacement and the outgoing diff.

Retry the push after removing the value from all affected commits. Do not bypass protection to publish
a recording containing a real credential.

For a confirmed false positive or an intentionally nonfunctional test value that cannot be replaced,
ask the maintainer to review the exact detection. Only the maintainer may authorize a bypass, with a
written reason and a link to the tracking issue. Never use an "I'll fix it later" bypass for a real secret.

Every alert has a deadline, counted in calendar days from the day it is created. Reading the alert, opening a follow-up issue, or asking for a fix does not stop the clock.

Dismissing an alert is a decision that has to survive being read a year later. An alert is dismissed only by the named person, only for a stated reason, and only when that reason is written down.

. A dismissal that does not name a person is not valid, and it is reversed at the next release review.
A dismissal is allowed for these reasons only:
The vulnerable package is only in a fixture or example manifest that is never installed, shipped, or run as the product's dependency.
The alert is wrong for this repository: no shipped lockfile resolves the vulnerable version, or the vulnerable code path is not reachable.
The maintainer accepts the risk in writing, with the condition under which the decision would change and a date to re-check it.
, or any reason that only means "not yet", is never used. Capacity is not a dismissal reason; an alert that cannot be fixed by its deadline stays open and overdue.

Write the dismissal comment on the alert first. It states the named person, the reason, the evidence (the manifest path and why the code is not shipped or reachable, or the accepted risk and review date), and a link to the pull request, issue, or release note that records the same reasoning.
Add a row to the dismissal log below with the same date, alert, package, reason, and person.
Dismiss the alert with that reason in the GitHub UI.
Every dismissal is reviewed at release.

When the baseline table above is updated for a release, each row in the dismissal log is re-read against the current manifests. A dismissal whose reason no longer holds is reversed: the alert is reopened and treated as new, with its deadline counted from the reopening date. A fixture that has become a shipped dependency is the usual cause.
